quickStart.title: Quick Start
quickStart.description: Add MCP Moira to your AI assistant. Choose your client below:

claude-web.description:
1. Go to claude.ai → Settings → Connectors
2. Click "Add custom connector"
3. Enter server URL and click "Connect"
4. Complete OAuth in browser

Requires Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise plan.

chatgpt.description:
1. Go to chat.openai.com → Settings → Connectors
2. Click "Add connector"
3. Enter name "MCP Moira" and server URL
4. Complete OAuth authentication

Requires Plus or Pro plan.

claude-code.authIntro: Then authenticate with your MCP Moira account:
claude-code.authContent:
Browser will open for OAuth authentication.
Authorize and return to terminal.

claude-desktop.description:
1. Open Settings (⌘+,) → Connectors tab
2. Click "Add custom connector"
3. Enter server URL and click "Connect"
4. Browser opens for OAuth → Done

No config file editing needed.

cursor.authIntro: Then authenticate with your MCP Moira account:
cursor.authContent:
Browser will open for OAuth authentication.
Authorize and return to Cursor.

vscode.authIntro: Then authenticate with your MCP Moira account:
vscode.authContent:
Browser will open for OAuth authentication.
Authorize and return to VS Code.

perplexity.description:
1. Install PerplexityXPC helper (Settings → Connectors → Install Helper)
2. Click "Add Connector"
3. Enter server name and MCP command
4. Complete OAuth authentication

Paid plan recommended. Uses mcp-remote bridge.

copilot-cli.authIntro: After saving the config file, authenticate:
copilot-cli.authContent:
1. Start a Copilot CLI session
2. Type /mcp
3. Select "moira" → Authenticate
→ Browser opens for OAuth

variables.guideBody: Every value here comes from the run's route: the variables the workflow declares and the fields each step returned. Open a variable's history to see which step changed it and when; edit a value in its row where the run allows it. Answering the waiting step or editing a variable acts on the run, never on the definition, and is recorded in the route as an adjustment with your name on it.

variables.adjustmentCount_one: {{count}} runtime adjustment recorded in the route
variables.adjustmentCount_other: {{count}} runtime adjustments recorded in the route
variables.fullscreen: Open the variables in a larger view

answer.title: Answer the waiting step
answer.body: The run is waiting at {{step}} in "{{block}}". Supply the evidence the step demands; Moira validates it like an agent's answer and continues the route.
answer.noFields: This step needs no fields: continuing records an empty answer.
answer.recorded: Recorded in the route as an adjustment by you.

cursor.hint: Drag to replay the run. The cursor is in the URL (at=), so a position can be linked to. Every mode shows block states as they were at the cursor, and the variables tab shows the values written up to it.

process.title: This is a process
process.body: A Moira workflow is a process: a sequence of named stages a piece of work goes through. We call each stage a block. The contents on the left lists them in order, and the highlighted row is one block: a status icon, a coloured number badge, the name, and how far the block has got. The same badge and name head that block's card on the diagram, in its title band.

agent.title: An agent runs it, one step at a time
agent.body: An AI agent executes the process. Inside every block are steps: one step is one instruction Moira hands the agent, with a condition for when it counts as done. Moira gives out exactly one step at a time; the agent cannot skip ahead. The highlight is the step the agent is on right now, in the Steps section of the block panel — click it and the panel opens the node level for that step, with a breadcrumb back to the block and its directive, completion condition, cases and connections in full.

evidence.title: It must return evidence
evidence.body: To finish a step, the agent must return evidence: the fields the step asks for, checked against a schema before Moira lets the run continue. The highlighted list is exactly what this step demands back; the Returns section of the node level names each field with its type and whether it is required. No matching evidence, no next step.

loop.title: A failed review sends the work back
loop.body: Some steps are reviews. When a review finds problems, the process does not continue: it returns to an earlier block, and the work is done again. That return is a loop. The highlight is a return port — the dashed pill marked ↻ on the card the work leaves from. It names the transition and where it goes; hover it to light the return line and read what causes the loop and what ends it, and click it to travel to the other end.

route.title: Every run leaves a route
route.body: A run is one execution of the process. Moira records its route: every step in order, every loop it went through, and the values the steps produced along the way. The highlight is this run's route cursor, in the toolbar of whichever view is open: drag it and the whole page — cards, panel and variables — goes back to that visit. The variables tab shows the values as they stood there, and any adjustment a person made is marked.

explore.title: Explore the same run your way
explore.body: The highlighted toolbar holds everything that changes what you see. The Map / Graph switch picks the view: the Map is the process with the run's state on it, the Graph is every step of the definition. The layout presets beside it re-lay both diagrams — rows, compact, balanced branches, top to bottom — and bring the camera back to the block you were reading. The magnifier finds a step by id or text, and the compass opens the note about the view that is open. Your selection and the camera survive a switch.

map.title: Map: the process as a diagram
map.body: Blocks run left to right in process order. A card opens with a title band — the block's number badge, its name and its status — and carries a column of input ports on the left and output ports on the right; a port names the transition and the block at the other end, and a click on it takes the camera there. A transition that sends the work back is a dashed return port marked ↻, and every transition a block makes to itself shares the double port under the card. Long links travel through the nearest free lane between rows instead of over the whole diagram. The card also carries the run's state: how many times the block ran, how long its passes took and, when it works through a list, how far that list has got — hover a fact chip, a port or a line to light it and read the rest. The contents on the left jumps to any block and its finder answers "which block is this step in"; the toolbar's layout presets re-lay the diagram and return the camera to the block you were reading.

graph.title: Graph: every step of the definition
graph.body: The same run, step by step: each block is a tinted group and each step inside it a card with the same title band, ports and fact chips as on the map. The chips carry the step's directive, the fields it must return and its expressions — hover one to read the full text in a tooltip. An output port is named by the case that selects it, `success` and `default` are the outputs taken when no case holds, and `error` and `timeout` are control outputs; return ports and the double port under a card mark the loops. The step the run is on breathes, the steps it has been through are toned as done. The contents on the left moves the camera to a block's group, the finder in the toolbar jumps to a step and opens its panel, and the layout presets re-lay the groups — stacked, compact, in a row, or with the steps turned top to bottom.

limits.description: What you can use, and how much of it you are using now.
limits.helpHeld: A codespace counts against your limit until it is deleted — stopping it keeps its files and its slot. Delete one you no longer need to free a slot.
limits.helpBilling: Codespaces are billed to your personal GitHub account. GitHub does not share billing or quota details with Moira; see them on GitHub.

autoPause.title: Automatic pause
autoPause.description: Stop codespaces agents are not using, so they do not keep running up your GitHub bill.
autoPause.helpCounts: Only what agents do through Moira: commands, file reads and writes, uploads and downloads. Moira does not see you working in a codespace directly in the browser, an editor or over SSH.
autoPause.helpResume: A paused codespace keeps its files. The next command an agent sends starts it again automatically.
autoPause.enableDescription: Stop a codespace after no agent has used it through Moira for the time below.
autoPause.timeoutDescription: How long a codespace may stay unused before it is paused.
autoPause.note: Only agent activity through Moira counts; direct use in the browser or an editor is not seen. If you work in your codespaces directly, turn this off. Either way, GitHub stops a codespace after at most 240 minutes without activity.

security.description: Your password and the browsers and devices currently signed in to your account.

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.description: Where Moira sends messages from your workflows, such as questions that need your answer.
notifications.helpBody: A workflow step can send you a message or ask you a question through a channel set up here. Each channel shows whether it is ready; send a test to check it.
notifications.helpTrusted: Trusted delivery lets a channel carry messages that unlock sensitive steps. An administrator must approve it for each channel.
notifications.emptyDescription: This Moira instance has no notification channels installed.

github.title: GitHub & Codespaces
github.description: Connect GitHub so agents can work in cloud codespaces for the repositories you choose.
github.helpTitle: What agents can do in a codespace
github.helpBody: A codespace is a cloud development machine for one of your repositories. Agents run commands and edit files in it through Moira's codespace tool; they never receive your GitHub credentials.
github.helpAuthority: Inside a codespace an agent has the same access as the codespace user: the repository, the network and any secrets configured for that codespace. Grant only repositories you are comfortable with.

apps.title: Connected apps
apps.description: AI assistants and other MCP clients you have allowed to use Moira with your account.
apps.helpBody: When an MCP client such as Claude or ChatGPT connects to Moira, you approve it on the Moira sign-in page. Each approval appears here with the permissions it received.
apps.helpRevoke: Revoking an app signs it out everywhere at once. It can connect again only after you approve it again.

tokens.title: API tokens
tokens.description: Long-lived keys for MCP clients and scripts that cannot use the browser sign-in.
tokens.helpTitle: When to use an API token
tokens.helpBody: Prefer connecting a client through the browser sign-in (see Connected apps). Use a token only for a client that cannot open a browser, such as a CI job or a headless agent.
tokens.helpHeader: The client sends the token in an HTTP header — Authorization: Bearer <token>.
tokens.helpOnce: A token is shown once, when you create it. Store it like a password; if it leaks, revoke it here.

preferences.title: Preferences
preferences.description: How the website looks and which language it uses in this browser.

preferences.themeDescription: Light, dark, or follow your system setting.
preferences.languageDescription: The language of the website's interface.

bot_token.label: Bot token
bot_token.description: The token @BotFather gave you when you created your bot.
bot_token.help: In Telegram, open @BotFather, send /newbot and follow the prompts. BotFather replies with a token like 123456:ABC-DEF…; paste it here. Moira stores it encrypted and never shows it again.

chat_id.label: Chat ID
chat_id.description: The chat Moira sends your messages to.
chat_id.help: In Telegram, find @userinfobot and send it any message: it replies with your user ID, which is your chat ID. Also send your own bot any message — Telegram lets a bot write to you only after that. Do not put the bot token into a browser URL: URLs can be retained in browser history, screenshots, proxies and logs.

enabled.label: Send notifications to Telegram
enabled.description: Turn off to pause Telegram messages without removing the bot.

nav.title: Jump between sections
nav.body: Every setting lives in one of these sections. Pick one to go straight to it; the section you are reading is marked as you scroll.

account.title: Your account
account.body: Your display name, email and username. The username is part of every workflow link you share, so change it with care.

security.title: Security & sign-in
security.body: Change your password and see every browser or device signed in to your account. Sign out any you do not recognise.

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.body: Set up where Moira reaches you, such as a Telegram bot, then send a test message to be sure it works.

github.title: GitHub & Codespaces
github.body: Connect GitHub and choose repositories so agents can work in cloud codespaces. Limits and automatic pausing are set here too.

apps.title: Connected apps
apps.body: AI assistants you have allowed to use Moira. Revoke any you no longer use.

tokens.title: API tokens
tokens.body: Keys for clients that cannot use the browser sign-in. A token is shown only once, when you create it.

preferences.title: Preferences
preferences.body: Choose the theme and language of the website. These apply in this browser.

steps.title: Three steps to connect
steps.body: Connect your GitHub account, install the Moira GitHub App, and grant it the repositories agents may work in. The current step is highlighted.

connect.title: Connect and install
connect.body: Press Connect GitHub and approve Moira on GitHub. If the Moira App is not installed yet, GitHub takes you straight to installing it; choose the repositories there. Back here, Check installation confirms it.

codespaces.title: Create a codespace
codespaces.body: Pick a repository and a branch, then create a codespace. Agents find it by its ID through the codespace tool. Stop keeps its files; Delete removes them.

limits.title: Know your limits
limits.body: How many codespaces you may hold (stopped ones count), how many commands can run at once and how much can be transferred. Delete a codespace you no longer need to free a slot.

autopause.title: Pause idle codespaces
autopause.body: Moira stops a codespace no agent has used through Moira for the time you choose, so it does not keep running up your GitHub bill. The next command starts it again.

bot.title: Create a bot
bot.body: In Telegram, message @BotFather, send /newbot and follow the prompts. Paste the token it gives you here and save.

chat.title: Find your chat ID
chat.body: Message @userinfobot in Telegram: the user ID it replies with is your chat ID. Paste it here and save, then send your own bot any message so it can write to you. Do not put the bot token into a browser URL.

enable.title: Turn it on
enable.body: Tick Send notifications to Telegram and save. The channel shows Ready when everything is in place.

test.title: Send a test

flowPage.title: Flow
flowPage.noProcess: This workflow declares no process view (no blocks), so the page shows its node graph. Add a `progress` section with blocks to read it as a process.

map.title: Map: the process as a diagram
map.body: Blocks run left to right in process order. A card opens with a title band — the block's number badge and its name — and carries a column of input ports on the left and output ports on the right; a port names the transition and the block at the other end, and a click on it takes the camera there. A transition that sends the work back is a dashed return port marked ↻, and every transition a block makes to itself shares the double port under the card; hover a port or a line to light it and read the condition, the cause and the exit of a loop. Long links travel through the nearest free lane between rows instead of over the whole diagram. The contents on the left jumps to any block and its finder answers "which block is this step in"; the toolbar's layout presets re-lay the diagram, and the panel on the right holds the block's description, its steps and, in edit mode, the authoring controls.

graph.title: Graph: every step of the definition
graph.body: The definition step by step: each block is a tinted group and each step inside it a card with the same title band, ports and fact chips as on the map. The chips carry the step's directive, the fields it must return and its expressions — hover one to read the full text in a tooltip. An output port is named by the case that selects it, `success` and `default` are the outputs taken when no case holds, and `error` and `timeout` are control outputs; return ports and the double port under a card mark the loops. Clicking a card opens the node level of the right panel, where the directive, the completion condition, the returned fields, the cases, the connections, the validation and a catalog-drawn node's configuration are read in full. The contents on the left moves the camera to a block's group, the finder in the toolbar jumps to a step, and the layout presets re-lay the groups — stacked, compact, in a row, or with the steps turned top to bottom.

registry.guideBody: Every global variable the workflow declares, with its type, description and default. Steps read them by name in their directives and conditions; a run's values appear on the run page. Undeclared names cannot be used.
registry.empty: This workflow declares no global variables.
registry.invalidJson: Not valid JSON — the previous default is kept until this parses.
registry.schema: Declaration as JSON Schema (type, description, default, enum, items, properties…)
registry.title: Declared variables

edit.hint: Edit mode changes the workflow definition itself — block names and descriptions, transition labels and loop explanations, which block a step belongs to, a step's directive or expressions, and the variable registry. It never touches a run. Edits live on the page until you save them; the save is refused if someone else changed the workflow in the meantime.
edit.guideTitle: You are editing the process definition
edit.guideBody: Change a block's name or description in place; click the pencil next to a transition to change its label or its loop's cause and exit; in the block panel, move a step to another block or edit its text; in Variables, edit the registry. Both views re-derive at once, rule violations appear as diagnostics, "Export" lists exactly which flow-file entries would change, and "Save" sends the definition to the server against the revision you loaded.
edit.conflict: Someone changed this workflow since you loaded it. Reload the page and apply your edits again.
edit.exportHint: Path in the workflow JSON, value before, value after — exactly what the save sends.
edit.label: Label

process.title: This is a process
process.body: A Moira workflow is a process: a sequence of named stages a piece of work goes through. We call each stage a block. The contents on the left lists them in order, and the highlighted row is one block: a coloured number badge, the name and how long the block usually takes. The same badge and name head that block's card on the diagram, in its title band.

agent.title: An agent runs it, one step at a time
agent.body: An AI agent executes the process. Inside every block are steps: one step is one instruction Moira hands the agent, with a condition for when it counts as done. Moira gives out exactly one step at a time; the agent cannot skip ahead. The highlight is one step of this block, in the Steps section of the block panel — click it and the page goes to that step on the graph and opens the node level of the panel, with its directive, completion condition, cases, connections and validation in full.

evidence.title: It must return evidence
evidence.body: To finish a step, the agent must return evidence: the fields the step asks for, checked against a schema before Moira lets the run continue. The highlighted list is exactly what this step demands back; the Returns section of the node level names each field with its type and whether it is required. No matching evidence, no next step.

loop.title: A failed review sends the work back
loop.body: Some steps are reviews. When a review finds problems, the process does not continue: it returns to an earlier block, and the work is done again. That return is a loop. The highlight is a return port — the dashed pill marked ↻ on the card the work leaves from. It names the transition and where it goes; hover it to light the return line and read what causes the loop and what ends it, and click it to travel to the other end.

edit.title: The definition can be edited here
edit.body: This page shows the definition, not a run: the header above names the flow, its version, its description and its facts, and carries the page's actions. Its owner can turn on edit mode to change block names and descriptions, transition labels, which block a step belongs to, a step's text and the variable registry; both views update at once and the save is checked by the server. Runs of this workflow are read on the run page.

explore.title: Explore the same process your way
explore.body: The highlighted toolbar holds everything that changes what you see. The Map / Graph switch picks the view: the Map is the process the workflow declares, the Graph is every step of the definition. The layout presets beside it re-lay both diagrams — rows, compact, balanced branches, top to bottom — and bring the camera back to the block you were reading. The magnifier finds a step by id or text, and the compass opens the note about the view that is open. Your selection and the camera survive a switch.
